title: Characterizing the Flammability of Nomex Fabric for the Preparation of FM<sup>2</sup>
abstract:
The Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM<sup>2</sup>) experiment will investigate, for the first time, the ignition, burning, and extinction characteristics of spacecraft materials in Lunar gravity on the surface of the Moon. Combustion experiments in drop towers, parabolic flights and space-based facilities (e.g., ISS) show that the gravity level has a significant effect on how materials burn. However, these facilities have significant limitations in providing an environment to simulate actual gravitational conditions on the Moon.

In the Artemis program, the cabin atmospheres will be comprised of elevated oxygen concentrations at reduced pressures to maintain normoxic conditions. This requires additional flammability testing, as materials considered safe to use on the ISS at Earth-normal oxygen concentration may be flammable in the Artemis cabin atmospheres on the Moon. In this study, combustion experiments using Nomex® HT-90 are designed to help guide the final selection of fuel, oxygen concentration, and ignition parameters for FM<sup>2</sup>. Several varieties of Nomex fabric are commonly used in spaceflight. Nomex is nonflammable on Earth in normal atmospheric conditions, however it burns in higher oxygen concentrations. 

Ignition and flame spread testing is performed in the NASA GRC 5.2 second drop tower, using a flow tunnel and a microgravity centrifuge to simulate the buoyant conditions. Normal 1-g ground tests are also conducted to support these drop tower experiments. During these tests, the oxygen levels and flow rates are varied to determine the optimal conditions for the materials to be tested on the surface of the Moon. The experiments show significant differences in the burning characteristics between 1-g with and without a concurrent flow, microgravity with a concurrent flow, and in Lunar gravity with no forced flow (but with Lunar buoyant flow).
